ca_echo_cove_north_side.blurb: A walled-in cove in the Echo Rock zone of Joshua Tree National Park, a short drive past Hidden Valley. The 22 climbs are mostly traditional crack and face lines on solid granite, with a pair of top-ropes and a single bolted line. Grades run from a couple of very easy scrambles through the 5.7 to 5.9 range up to a handful of 5.11s, so there is something for beginners leading cracks and for stronger climbers alike. Getting to the rock takes only minutes, which suits a quick morning session before the desert heat builds. Expect a lot of company, since the cove is easy to reach and well liked for top-roping.

ca_summit_or_plummet_rock.blurb: A small formation among the roadside crags on the west side of Park Boulevard in Joshua Tree National Park's Hidden Valley district, roughly midway between Glory Dome and the pavement and an easy stroll from the car. Its east face carries most of the 22 routes, nearly all of them trad with a couple of top-rope options. Difficulty spreads from about 5.5 to 5.12, with the bulk sitting around 5.8 to 5.10, so it works for a mixed party warming up on shorter lines. Climbs are brief, in the range of a single rope length or less, which makes it a handy stop between bigger objectives rather than a full-day destination.

ca_ad_arch_rock.blurb: A big, stepped granite cliff beside the Highway 140 entrance to Yosemite, in the lower Merced River Canyon. Climbing here is mostly traditional, with a few bolted lines, and the 22 routes start at 5.9 and run up through 5.12, with the greatest share at 5.11. Several are multi-pitch, so this suits confident leaders with a full rack. The canyon sits at lower elevation than the Valley floor and its weather can differ noticeably, which makes it an option when higher walls are cold. Reaching the base means a scramble up talus.

ca_cardinal_pinnacle.blurb: A tall granite pinnacle of roughly 400 to 500 feet above the Bishop Creek road, west of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra at around 9,200 feet. It is a crack climber's cliff: steep, exposed splitters on clean rock, with nearly all of the 22 routes traditional and a lone bolted line. Grades start near 5.6 for an approachable moderate way up, but most of the climbing falls at 5.10 and 5.11, with a few 5.12s and a 5.13. The west face collects full sun by midday, and the cliff draws plenty of climbers, especially on busy weekends. Bring a double set of cams.
ca_cardinal_pinnacle.parking_note: Use the roadside pull-off along Highway 168 just above Aspendell, on the left when heading up the canyon, and start up the talus slope from there.

ca_waterway_west.blurb: A section of the Labyrinth, the maze of limestone boulders near Columbia in the Sierra foothills, off the Sonora Pass highway. The 22 problems range from the easiest grades through V7, with the greatest cluster in the V3 to V6 band and a few harder lines on top. This is adventure bouldering: tight corridors, some tall problems and uneven landings, so bring several pads and a spotter. The Labyrinth is famously confusing to navigate, and a map or local help is wise. Cool months suit it best, and the rock tends to dry quickly after rain, although low spots near the water can stay wet.

ca_green_phantom_rock.blurb: A modest granite cliff on Donner Summit, tucked directly under the old arched bridge at about 6,800 feet and looking out over Donner Lake. It is not tall, but the rock is good quality and the holds can feel small and slippery, which makes it a fair test of footwork. The 22 routes include a mix of trad, top-rope and a few sport lines, with grades from about 5.5 up to 5.11 and the largest group at 5.10. Many lines are easy to top-rope, which makes this a favorite of instructors and groups, so expect company on nice days.

ca_snickers_south_face.blurb: The sunny south side of the Snickers formation in the Echo Rock district of Joshua Tree National Park, near Barker Dam Road. The face looks somewhat broken from a distance but holds a good set of lines, mostly trad with a few bolted routes, a top-rope and one aid climb. Difficulty leans hard: a block of 5.11s makes up the majority, with a few 5.12s, plus some easier climbs from 5.7 to 5.9. A box canyon partway along the wall gives shelter from the wind, and the face sees light traffic, so it is a calm choice on a blustery day.
ca_snickers_south_face.approach: Follow the usual trail toward Little Rock Candy Mountain, then continue east about 100 m along the base of the formation. Turn north at the box canyon to reach the routes there; a little scrambling is involved. The routes further east sit on higher ledges and start from easy blocks and slabs.
